newsitem.title: UK: International LPG firm, India tenders for big volume.
newsitem.headline: International LPG firm, India tenders for big volume.

text.p: Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) prices were steady to firm in all centres this week.

Strong prices in the U.S. continued to draw cargoes from Europe despite high inventories, North Sea levels rose towards the end of the week, and a huge Indian tender was expected to give support to levels in Asia.

The Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) tendered for 540,000 tonnes spread over a year, split into 18 cargoes each of 25,000 tonnes of butane and 5,000 tonnes of propane. They are for delivery between July and June next year, at the rate of three cargoes every two months, and the tender is open until May 27.

One trader was sceptical the tender would be awarded at all, pointing out that it is impossible for bidders to predict LPG levels so far ahead. As a result, bids are likely to be pitched at a high enough level to protect sellers, and the IOC may find it more attractive to buy product on a spot basis over the year or increase current contract volumes rather than pay what may turn out to be high prices for a term tender.

But a Japanese trader said the tender was expected to boost butane prices, although the market has become opaque recently, with little spot activity seen out of the Middle East. He said that the IOC tender has not caused a price spike, but added that butane's value seems "a bit higher" in the light of the huge requirement.

Further east, Japanese and Korean buyers are still "watching the market," a trader said. Buyers there traditionally build stocks in the summer to meet peak winter demand, and they try to buy at the bottom of the market. There is little enthusiasm seen for buying in May against the May Contract Price (CP), the Saudi benchmark price against which LPG in markets east of Suez is priced, as dealers expect the CP to fall significantly in June.
But a trader said that there have been recent indications from sellers that June CP +$11 a tonne C+F Japan may be a realistic price for propane, and some buyers appeared interested at this price.
"May trade seems unlikely," he said. "People still think the June CP will be lower. There is some risk, but it is considered a minor risk."

In Europe, North Sea propane prices came up towards the end of the week. A large cargo was reported done at around $178 or $179 a tonne cif Scandinavia, and another 10,000 tonne cargo was reported done above $180 a tonne cif NWE for loading around May 17.
"It's very strange, deals are getting done well above naphtha parity which is surprising at this time of year," said a trader.

He said there was a general tightness of product and that with stocks already running down ahead of the summer, any spell of cold weather is reflected almost immediately in a brief price spike, even if turns out to be short-lived.

Small sea-going propane coasters were also firm, with prices rising into the low $190's a tonne fob UK. A dealer said that demand from Portugal, cold weather and a general shortage of product had tightened the market. A seller in the Mediterranean reported selling a 3,000 tonne cargo at over $210 cif North France on Friday morning, consistent with fob prices for coasters in the region.

But while propane remains strong, butane is not so lively in Northwest Europe. A Scandinavian producer sold a 40,000 tonne parcel to the U.S. mid-week, mostly butane but with some propane on board as well. The European butane market is described as dead, with the seller of the large trans-Atlantic cargo saying "you can't sell it in Europe now."
A coaster trader agreed that butane is now starting to show weakness, and added that product is moving to Brazil as the demand from Europe is not there.

In the Mediterranean, the region's biggest seller said that it was continuing to send the maximum possible LPG volumes to the U.S., where consistent strength makes it a more attractive market than Europe despite the late pick-up in North Sea propane prices.

There were unconfirmed reports that a propane piece had been traded at around $200 a tonne cif northern Italy, into a port which commands a premium over the major Mediterranean terminal of Lavera in southern France. Propane at Lavera itself was notionally assessed at $180/$190 a tonne, with butane seen lower. But the butane price is somewhat notional given that the regional market is even less liquid than for propane.

In the U.S., propane inventories recorded their largest April stockbuild since 1993, the Energy Information Administration (EIA) said on Thursday. Stocks rose by 6.1 million barrels to 32.2 million as of April 30. But despite this, short-covering requirements and support from NYMEX futures kept prices up, and the influx of foreign cargoes, especially from Algeria, showed no sign of abating by the end of the week.
